questions.q: {p} earns {r} compound interest a year for {y} years. What's the final balance?
questions.why: {p} × (1 + {r})^{y} = {answer}. Each year's interest is added before the next year's is worked out.

questions.topic: interest on interest vs total interest
questions.q: {p} earns {r} compound interest a year for {y} years. How much of the interest is interest on interest (the extra compared with simple interest)?
questions.why: Total interest is {total}. Simple interest would be {simple}. The difference, {answer}, is interest earned on interest. It isn't next year's interest.

questions.q: Using the rule of 72, roughly how many years does money take to double at {r} a year?
questions.why: 72 ÷ {r} = {answer} years. Halve the rate and the time doubles.

questions.q: Your savings pay 4.5% and inflation is 3.5%. Roughly what's your real return?
questions.why: Inflation works against you, so subtract it: 4.5 − 3.5 ≈ 1%. Adding it (8%) is the classic mistake.

questions.q: An account pays {r} a year and inflation is {i}. Roughly what's the real return, in %? (Use a minus sign if it's negative.)
questions.why: Real ≈ {r} − {i}. Exactly: (1 + {r}) ÷ (1 + {i}) − 1 = {answer}%. Subtract inflation, never add it.

questions.q: If your savings balance goes up, you're always better off.
questions.why: Only if your rate beats inflation. A 1% account with 3.5% inflation grows in pounds but buys less.

questions.topic: why time matters most (more years at the end)
questions.q: Explain why starting to save at 18 rather than 28 makes such a big difference, even with the same money and the same rate.

ideas.label: The earlier money gets more years to grow, and the last years grow the most

questions.model: Money saved earlier gets more years of interest earning interest. Growth is biggest in the final years, when the pot is largest, so starting at 28 cuts off the most valuable years at the end. The time matters more than the amount.
questions.why: Compounding is the mechanism; extra years (especially the big final ones) are the reason it matters.

tests.answer: Money you save at 18 gets ten more years of interest earning interest, and the last years grow the most.
Because of compound interest the money will compound and beat it.
At 18 you have less money so it doesn't really matter.

questions.q: A friend says their savings account paying 1% is safe because the balance never goes down. Inflation is 3.5%. What would you tell them?

ideas.label: Prices are rising faster than their interest (inflation is higher than 1%)
So the money loses spending power / real value

questions.model: They're right about the pounds but wrong about the value. Inflation is 3.5%, so prices are rising faster than their money grows at 1%. It loses about 2.4% of its spending power a year. A better-paying account keeps the same safety and shrinks the loss.
questions.why: Safe in pounds isn't safe in spending power.

tests.answer: Inflation is 3.5% so prices rise faster than the 1% interest, meaning their money buys less each year.
They are right, banks are safe and protected.

questions.q: The Bank of England raises Bank Rate. What usually happens next?
options: Savings and borrowing rates both tend to rise
Savings rates rise and borrowing rates fall
Borrowing rates rise and savings rates fall
questions.why: Other rates follow Bank Rate. Borrowing rates often move quickly; savings rates can lag because many savers never switch.

questions.q: Inflation is 3.5%. Put these places for £1,500 in order of spending power after one year, most first.
questions.why: The higher the rate, the more spending power. Only the accounts above 3.5% gain any; cash at home loses about 3.4%.

pairs: The main UK measure of inflation
